new_articles.title: Assembly and testing of aqueous organic redox flow batteries
new_articles.abstract: Aqueous organic redox flow batteries (AORFBs) are a class of scalable, safe and sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems. However, the lack of standardized protocols for the synthesis, assembly and testing of organic redox-active materials has impeded reproducibility and comparability across the field. Here we present a comprehensive protocol for the design, fabrication and electrochemical evaluation of AORFBs using phenazine- and fluorenone-based anolytes as model systems (for example, 7,8-dihydroxyphenazine-2-sulfonic acid (DHPS) and 4-carboxylic-7-sulfonate fluorenone (4C7S-FL)). This protocol details the synthesis of these compounds, pre-treatment of cation exchange membranes, assembly of a modular 10 cm2 interdigitated flow cell, preparation of alkaline aqueous electrolytes and standardized battery testing procedures—including electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, constant current cycling, rate capability and constant voltage (chronoamperometry). The protocol integrates custom lab-scale flow cell designs that we have previously demonstrated preserve key hydrodynamic characteristics of large-area 780-cm2 kilowatt-scale stacks, enabling meaningful performance translation. Representative results for DHPS and 4C7S-FL include Coulombic efficiencies exceeding 99%, energy efficiencies over 90% and capacity fade rates below 0.01% per cycle. This protocol provides step-by-step guidance to facilitate the reproducible benchmarking of organic AORFBs and supports the broader adoption of flow batteries in grid-scale energy storage. The procedure requires intermediate expertise in synthetic chemistry and electrochemical testing and cell assembly and testing can be completed over 2–4 d depending on scope once prerequisite materials have been synthesized.

new_articles.title: Optimized oviductal injection protocol for i-GONAD using electric microinjectors
new_articles.abstract: The improved Genome Editing via Oviductal Nucleic Acids Delivery (i-GONAD) method enables the generation of genetically engineered animals by delivering genome-editing reagents to fertilized eggs present in the oviducts of pregnant female mice through in vivo electroporation, without the need to euthanize the female or retrieve embryos for ex vivo manipulations. A key step in this technique involves injecting the solution into the oviduct, which has traditionally been performed using a mouth-operated glass capillary system. However, this method has several practical limitations. First, mouth pipetting is technically demanding, particularly for inexperienced researchers. Specifically, precise control of aspiration and dispensing of very small volumes requires substantial practice. Second, mouth pipetting may not be ideal for maintaining strict specific pathogen-free conditions in some animal facilities. In addition, mouth pipetting may raise biosafety concerns owing to potential exposure of researchers to reagents, which can limit the use of the i-GONAD for delivering biohazardous agents such as viral vectors. Here we optimize and extend the i-GONAD protocol by introducing electric microinjectors as an alternative tool for reagent delivery into the mouse oviduct. We also present optimized injection parameters using this system. The Protocol can be completed in ~2 d, including 1 d for mating and 1 d for the i-GONAD procedure. This timeline does not include the steps performed before the procedure (design and preparation of genome-editing reagents) or after the procedure (analysis of genome-editing outcomes).

new_articles.title: Ammonia electrosynthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen
new_articles.abstract: Ammonia is essential for the fertilizer and chemical industries and is increasingly valued as a carbon-free fuel. Electrochemical ammonia synthesis under ambient conditions offers a decentralized and sustainable alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process, which requires high temperature, high pressure and large centralized plants. Among emerging strategies, the lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction has shown exceptional promise for ambient-condition ammonia electrosynthesis. This Protocol describes a continuous ammonia electrosynthesis method that combines a lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction with the hydrogen oxidation reaction in a flow cell operating at ambient temperature and pressure. In this system, metallic lithium is deposited on the cathode, where it forms a solid electrolyte interphase. The metallic lithium activates N2 to form lithium nitrides or dissociated nitrogen species, which are subsequently protonated to produce ammonia. Protons are sustainably sourced by the hydrogen oxidation reaction at the anode using a PtAu alloy catalyst. We provide detailed procedures for anode catalyst synthesis, electrolyte preparation and solid electrolyte interphase tuning, flow-cell assembly, continuous ammonia electrosynthesis, and the use of electrochemical in situ spectroscopy to probe reaction mechanisms. Compared with conventional approaches, this continuous ammonia electrosynthesis strategy offers multiple advantages as a sustainable alternative, including operational simplicity, long-term stability and high Faradaic efficiency. This protocol can be performed by researchers with standard training in electrochemistry and basic experience in handling air-sensitive materials, assembling electrochemical flow cells and operating gas-flow systems. The core protocol takes ~65 h to complete, with an additional ~34 h required for mechanistic characterization, including operando mass spectrometry, isotope studies and cryogenic transmission electron microscopy analysis.

new_articles.title: Precise large-scale DNA manipulations in plants using engineered site-specific recombinase-based programmable chromosome engineering technology
new_articles.abstract: Although genome-editing technologies have advanced at breakneck pace, rapid development in the life sciences field continues to place increasingly higher demands on them. Next-generation genome-editing tools must be capable of performing precise chromosomal-scale DNA manipulations, including insertions, replacements, deletions, inversions and translocations. Recently, systems for precise large-scale genome editing in plants have been developed, demonstrating considerably higher accuracy and efficiency than traditional nonhomologous end joining-mediated approaches. These technologies are collectively referred to as programmable chromosome engineering (PCE) and utilize an engineered plant prime editor for flexible programming of recombination sites, insertion positions and orientations, followed by precise large-scale DNA recombination with an iterative site-specific recombinase system. Here we describe a protocol for implementing PCE in plants. We outline a workflow for PCE-mediated editing, including target site design using the PCE Targets Designer web tool, vector construction, evaluation of editing efficiency via droplet digital PCR and plant transformation for generating desired mutants. Using this workflow, editing can be assessed within 5–9 days, and PCE-edited plants can be obtained within 3–5 months.

new_articles.title: Differential transcript expression and differential transcript usage using Salmon and edgeR
new_articles.abstract: Differential transcript expression (DTE) and differential transcript usample information and experimentalsage (DTU) analyses provide high-resolution insights into transcript-level changes and regulatory mechanisms. Here we present a protocol built around the recently developed edgeR DTE and DTU frameworks, which incorporate quantification-uncertainty correction and new quasi-likelihood methods that have been demonstrated to outperform alternative tools in statistical power, false discovery rate control and computational efficiency. These methods are general and can be applied to any well-annotated reference transcriptome. To illustrate the workflow, we apply the protocol using the complete telomere-to-telomere (T2T-CHM13) human reference genome, whose improved assembly and transcript annotation offer enhanced accuracy for transcript-level analyses of human samples. The protocol uses Salmon for fast transcript quantification, incorporates strategies for organizing GFF-based annotations and employs edgeR for assessing DTE and DTU while accounting for read-to-transcript ambiguity and variation between biological replicates. Applying the workflow to an RNA-sequencing dataset from human lung adenocarcinoma cell lines, we show that the combination of Salmon and edgeR reliably identifies differentially expressed or differentially used transcripts between experimental conditions. The end-to-end protocol can be completed in under 2 h for quantification in Salmon and less than 10 min for statistical analysis in edgeR. It provides a flexible, high-performance framework for transcript-level analyses across diverse organisms and reference genomes and can be carried out by researchers with basic experience using the Unix command line and R.

new_articles.title: Predictive modeling of single-cell transcriptomic dynamics with Dynamo
new_articles.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a powerful means to investigate cell fate dynamics during development and disease. However, existing computational approaches—such as RNA velocity—are often limited to qualitative and descriptive insights. We previously presented Dynamo, a machine learning framework that leverages noisy RNA velocity estimates to learn analytical and predictive vector fields of gene expression dynamics. These learned vector fields enable a suite of novel, quantitative analyses, including mapping the geometry of cell state transitions, identifying dynamic features of differentiation trajectories, inferring gene regulatory networks, predicting optimal paths and transcription factor cocktails for cellular reprogramming, and simulating in silico genetic perturbations. Here we provide a comprehensive protocol for applying Dynamo across four distinct data types and five downstream analyses, demonstrating its versatility in handling conventional and metabolic-labeling-enabled scRNA-seq, multiomic datasets and even datasets without velocity information. We also show that Dynamo can predict cell fate diversions following genetic perturbations and accurately identify key transcription factors that enable lineage transitions in the hematopoietic system. By enabling predictive modeling from single-cell data, our protocol aims to empower the development of generative and predictive models of single-cell genomics. While typical RNA velocity vector field analyses can be completed in less than an hour, the nine case studies in the Protocol can be completed in ~7 h and 35 min. The Protocol is designed for researchers with basic familiarity in scRNA-seq analysis and Python programming, although no advanced coding expertise is required.

new_articles.title: A robotics- and machine learning-integrated workflow for discovering all-natural plastic substitutes
new_articles.abstract: The global accumulation of nondegradable petrochemical plastic waste is driving the search for biodegradable substitutes derived from natural resources. However, discovering all-natural composite materials that match the optical, thermal and mechanical performance of commercial plastics remains challenging because traditional iterative optimization is inefficient. Here the workflow described in this Protocol accelerates the screening process by using automated robotics for liquid handing and machine learning to predict material properties. The procedure begins by commanding a pipetting robot to prepare a library of 286 nanocomposites. Basic physical properties of these products are used to train a support vector machine classifier that locates the decision boundary separating feasible from infeasible film compositions in the four-component system, thereby defining the feasible design space. Next, through 14 active learning loops coupled with data augmentation (for example, adding small random changes to the characterization data within the observed experimental error range), the robot fabricates 135 all-natural nanocomposites in a stagewise manner to construct an artificial neural network prediction model. The model is used to predict (1) the physicochemical properties of a nanocomposite from its composition and (2) which compositions are likely to have the desired, user-specified properties (for example, transparency or fire resistance). This protocol further details methods for model interpretation using Shapley Additive Explanations, validation via molecular dynamics simulations and model expansion to incorporate new building blocks. This hybrid approach takes ~2 months and enables the accelerated discovery of eco-friendly materials with programmable functions using components drawn from the generally recognized as safe database.

new_articles.title: Detection and characterization of in cellulo protein–RNA complexity by irCLIP-RNP, irCLIPv2 and Re-CLIP
new_articles.abstract: Transcriptome-wide methods to map RNA–protein interactions in living cells provide powerful tools to unravel the complexity of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies and their roles in post-transcriptional regulation. Here, we present three interconnected cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP)-based procedures, irCLIP-RNP, irCLIPv2 and Re-CLIP, that enable the identification and characterization of RNA-dependent associated proteins (RDAPs) in proximity to a target RNA-binding protein (RBP). After the construction of the infrared (IR) biotinylated DNA adapter, these methods combine UV cross-linking, partial RNase digestion, protein-specific immunoprecipitation and 3′ DNA adapter ligation, followed by distinct downstream workflows: mass spectrometry for RDAP identification (irCLIP-RNP), RNA sequencing to map binding regions (irCLIPv2) or a second immunoprecipitation with sequencing for interaction validation (Re-CLIP). Custom bioinformatics pipelines analyze enriched RDAPs or significant binding sites, offering mechanistic insights into proximal RNA–protein interactions. Compared to conventional CLIP methods, these protocols resolve adjacent interactions, linking RBPs to their RDAPs with greater precision. The workflow is applicable across diverse contexts such as cell state transitions and stimulus responses. It requires expertise in RNA biochemistry, next-generation sequencing and computational analysis. The entire process, from cell harvesting to data analysis, can be completed in 7–10 d, providing a robust toolkit for investigating post-transcriptional regulatory networks.

new_articles.title: Personalization and evaluation of human whole-body metabolic models and community microbiome models using Persephone
new_articles.abstract: Human metabolism and human gut microbiome co-metabolism can be difficult to investigate in vivo owing to the complexity of the systems involved. Genome-scale metabolic modeling with human whole-body metabolic models (WBMs) offers a computational approach to address this challenge. However, personalization and analysis of WBMs requires comprehensive knowledge of metabolic modeling, which can be daunting for beginners. To reduce the computational expertise required and to standardize the process of working with and analyzing WBMs, we present Persephone: a personalization and evaluation pipeline for human WBMs. Persephone has functionalities to create community microbiome models from raw sequencing data or taxonomy-assigned read tables, use physiological and metabolomic data to create personalized WBMs, combine community microbiome models with WBMs or personalized WBMs to create community microbiome (personalized) WBMs, optimize WBMs according to user-defined metabolic reactions, perform statistical analyses to describe the data, and visualize significant results in various figures. Persephone saves intermediate results as well as a log file with all changes made to the model, data and any warnings encountered during the various steps. Persephone is designed for use by anyone with basic research-computing experience and access to modest computer hardware. Applications include the investigation of human–microbiome co-metabolism and the evaluation of the effects of various physiological parameters, such as weight, on human metabolism. Using a dataset of 100 metagenomic samples, it can take several days to a week to run Persephone on a single computer, depending on the number of reactions optimized and whether taxonomic assignment is performed.
